Name: numeral_structure_arithmetic
Title: Does 'Ninety' Compute Differently from 'Quatre-Vingt-Dix'? Language-Specific Numeral Grammar as a Hidden Tax on Multilingual Arithmetic
Short Hypothesis: Number words encode arithmetic structure differently across languages (English/Chinese are decimal-transparent; French/Danish are partly vigesimal, e.g. 'quatre-vingt-dix' = 4x20+10; Hindi has opaque, irregular teen/tens forms). We hypothesize that when a multilingual LLM reads a number as a *word* (not digits), the compositional structure of that language's numeral system leaks into the model's internal magnitude representation and causally affects arithmetic accuracy: vigesimal/irregular numeral languages induce systematically more errors and a distorted, non-linear internal number line, even though the underlying quantity is identical. We further hypothesize a shared, language-agnostic 'digit-magnitude' representation exists, and that mapping word-form numbers onto it (via a training-free steering or transliteration-to-digits intervention) removes the numeral-grammar tax.
Related Work: Prior work shows LLMs encode numeric magnitude on an approximately linear 'number line' in the residual stream (Zhu et al. 2024; interpretability of arithmetic circuits, e.g., Nikankin et al. 2024 'arithmetic without algorithms'), and that multilingual models share vs. specialize neurons across languages. Cross-lingual math work (MGSM) measures reasoning accuracy across languages but treats numbers as translated tokens and attributes gaps to resource level. Tokenization work notes digit chunking effects on arithmetic. What is missing: a controlled study isolating the *linguistic structure of numeral systems themselves* (decimal-transparent vs. vigesimal vs. irregular) as a causal factor in internal magnitude representation and arithmetic, disentangled from resource level and from digit tokenization. No prior work links numeral-word grammar to distortions of the internal number line or offers a mechanistic remedy. This is a simple, elegant, and novel probe of language-specific vs. shared quantity representation.
Abstract: Every language has words for numbers, but the grammar of those words differs radically: English and Mandarin are decimal-transparent (ninety = 9 tens), French and Danish are partly vigesimal (quatre-vingt-dix = four-twenties-ten), and many languages have irregular teen and tens forms. When a multilingual LLM reads a number written as a word rather than as digits, does the compositional structure of that numeral system leak into how the model represents the quantity, and does this affect its arithmetic? We hypothesize a numeral-grammar tax: languages whose number words are non-transparent induce a distorted internal 'number line' and systematically higher arithmetic error, holding the actual quantity constant. We test this across four open multilingual models using a controlled battery of numbers rendered as digits versus as words in ten languages spanning decimal-transparent, vigesimal, and irregular numeral systems, matched for magnitude and resource level. First, we probe the residual-stream magnitude representation for each rendering and measure linearity/monotonicity of the recovered number line by language. Second, we measure arithmetic accuracy (comparison, addition) on word-form versus digit-form inputs and regress errors on numeral-transparency features. Third, using activation patching, we test whether the model reconstructs a shared digit-magnitude representation for word inputs, and where; and we introduce a training-free repair that maps word-form numbers onto the shared digit representation. We report per-language number-line distortion, the transparency-vs-error relationship controlling for confounds, the causal locus of numeral parsing, and accuracy recovery from the intervention. This reframes a slice of multilingual math gaps as a consequence of numeral grammar rather than missing knowledge.
Experiments: 1) Numeral typology setup: Select 10 languages grouped by numeral-system type — decimal-transparent (English, Mandarin, Turkish, Swahili), vigesimal/partly-vigesimal (French, Danish, Georgian, Basque), and irregular/opaque tens-teens (Hindi, Bengali). Assign each language a quantitative 'numeral transparency' score (e.g., rule-based: presence of vigesimal bases, irregularity/entropy of tens-forms, additive vs. multiplicative composition). 2) Stimuli: For numbers 11–99 (and an extension to 100–999), generate correct number-word spellings per language (using verified numeral-spelling libraries / native or MT verification) and a matched digit rendering. This holds magnitude constant across languages, isolating word-form structure. 3) Number-line probing: On open models (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Aya-23-8B, Gemma-2-9B), extract last-token mid-layer residual activations for each word-form number; fit a linear probe / regression to recover magnitude and measure R^2, monotonicity violations, and reconstruction error, per language. Compare word-form vs. digit-form number-line quality. Hypothesis: transparency score correlates with number-line linearity (Spearman). 4) Arithmetic behavior: Two tasks — (a) magnitude comparison ('Is X larger than Y?') and (b) two-operand addition, with operands presented as words in each language and answers scored by normalization. Regress error rate on numeral transparency, magnitude, and a language-resource covariate; test whether transparency predicts errors beyond resource level. Include a control where operands are digits but the prompt language varies (isolates numeral-word structure from prompt language). 5) Causal mechanism: Use activation patching / logit-lens to test whether/where word-form numbers get remapped to a shared digit-magnitude representation; patch the digit-form representation of the same number into the word-form run and test if arithmetic accuracy is restored. Sweep layers to localize numeral parsing. 6) Training-free repair: Two interventions — (i) preprocess by transliterating word-form numbers to digits before the operation (behavioral upper bound), and (ii) an internal steering that injects the shared digit-magnitude representation at the localized layer; measure accuracy recovery on high-tax languages and specificity (no degradation on transparent languages / digit inputs). Metrics: number-line R^2 and monotonicity per language, transparency–error partial correlation, patching recovery rate, layer-localization curves, repair accuracy delta and specificity.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Numeral transparency and language resource level may be correlated; we mitigate with the magnitude-matched design (identical quantities across languages), a within-model digit-vs-word contrast, and explicit resource covariates, and report residual confounding. 2) Digit tokenization idiosyncrasies could confound; we control by comparing to digit-form baselines and by fixing the digit rendering. 3) Correct numeral spellings for some languages are nontrivial; we use verified numeral libraries plus native/MT checks and audit a sample. 4) Number-line probing can conflate magnitude with token frequency; we include frequency covariates and validate probes on held-out numbers. 5) Activation-patching localization is model-specific; we report across four models and sweep layers. 6) A null result (numeral grammar has no effect; models fully normalize word-forms to a shared representation) is itself a clean, informative finding about language-agnostic quantity representation. 7) Effects may shrink for very common small numbers; we stratify by magnitude to find where the tax is largest.
